questions.q: Why is ScrapReasonID left nullable all the way from stg.WorkOrder through to dw.FactWorkOrder.ScrapReasonKey?
options: Most work orders scrap nothing at all, so a valid row can legitimately arrive with no scrap reason
Production.WorkOrder never actually populates this column
SQL Server requires every foreign key column to be nullable
It's a data entry mistake that should be fixed in staging
questions.explain: A work order that produced its full quantity with zero scrap has no scrap reason to record — that's a normal, valid case, not missing data to clean up.

questions.q: Why is dw.DimScrapReason built as an SCD Type 0 dimension instead of Type 1 or Type 2?
options: It's a small, essentially static reference table — Production.ScrapReason rarely changes, so there's no history worth tracking and no meaningful 'overwrite' scenario to handle
Type 0 dimensions are required for every dimension smaller than 100 rows
SQL Server doesn't support IDENTITY columns on Type 1 dimensions
DimScrapReason needs to track full historical change, which only Type 0 supports
questions.explain: Type 0 is the honest choice for a small, essentially static reference table — pretending it needs Type 2 history tracking would be over-engineering it.

questions.q: Why does this capstone reference an existing dw.DimDate table instead of building a new one?
options: DimDate is a conformed dimension — building it once and reusing it (including three times on one fact table) avoids duplicating a calendar table that should always agree with itself
SQL Server only allows one date dimension per database
AdventureWorks2012 has no date data to build a dimension from
dw.DimDate must be rebuilt from scratch for every new fact table
questions.explain: A conformed DimDate, built once, is exactly what lets Lesson 6 reference it three separate times as three different roles without three separate ETL loads to keep in sync.

questions.q: What is the key structural difference between the stg schema and the dw schema, even though both live on the same SQL Server instance?
options: stg uses wide, forgiving types with no constraints and is disposable; dw uses strict types, surrogate keys, and primary/foreign key constraints, and is the durable version other tools read from
stg and dw are functionally identical and exist only for naming preference
dw tables are always temporary and get dropped after each load
stg tables use foreign keys to enforce data quality; dw tables never do
questions.explain: The schema separation makes the distinction between disposable scratch space and the durable, report-facing warehouse visible in every object name.

questions.q: What key type does dw.DimProduct's ProductAlternateKey column represent?
options: The original OLTP natural key (Production.Product.ProductID), kept so ETL can look up the dimension row during a load
A brand-new surrogate key generated only for reporting
A foreign key to dw.FactWorkOrder
A randomly generated GUID unrelated to any source system
questions.explain: ProductAlternateKey preserves the real source ProductID so the SSIS Lookup transformation in Lesson 4 has something concrete to match against.
